title: No more excuses. It’s time to open.
html:
Last year I wrote about the challenges of getting organizations to open their data, and the need for creative data sharing and open humanitarianism. Since that time, Leandro Salazar-Liévano and I worked to draft the Open Humanitarianism concept. Lauren Parater and Hildemar Cruz helped to act as a sounding board. And, my wife Andrea, took on some heavy lifting by designing the logo, developing & designing the website and turning the 50-pages of content into web-ready material.

Inspired by the Open Government movement, Open Humanitarianism lays out a framework that humanitarian organizations can use to help open themselves, to become more responsive to those they serve, to share data freely (and securely), and to transform themselves into transparent entities.  By becoming open, humanitarian organizations will help affected populations to have the information that will allow them to make informed decisions about their lives. These organizations will also contribute to an environment of tolerance, openness, honesty and transparency, which offers a shield against corruption and abuse of power.

The Open Humanitarianism framework consists of four pillars:

  1. Transparency
  2. Collaboration
  3. Participation
  4. Accountability

It also provides a mechanism for humanitarian organizations to publicly commit to being open. Organizations can apply to use the Open Humanitarianism logo as a symbol that their organization has taken concrete steps to being transparent, collaborative, participatory and accountable.

One of these steps is signing the Open Humanitarian Data Declaration [PDF]. In endorsing the declaration, an organization acknowledges that opening its data is key to improving humanitarian response.

On behalf of those who passionately believe that an open humanitarian community will better serve the needs of the affected population, I hope that the Open Humanitarianism framework can help usher in a new era for the sector.

Andrej
teaser: No more excuses: introducing Open Humanitarianism, a concept for opening humanitarian data developed with Leandro Salazar-Liévano.
